2017_106_041817mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of April 18, 2017 at the Services Building — a technology-buying meeting. The Board awards $718,743.85 of classroom A/V displays to VSC and $406,473.00 of district-wide synchronized clocks to Sound Engineering, both from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, plus $201,380.00 of flooring replacement and a three-year district-wide refuse collection contract to GFL Environmental. It recognizes 38 nominees for the Outstanding Teacher Award, hears Smith Middle School's "U-Knighted Hour" program, and receives the Superintendent's World Class by 2020 update.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, April 18, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment is Smith Middle School's **"U-Knighted Hour."** Over the previous summer a group of Smith teachers met to develop a homeroom for all students, the building having recognized a need for a stronger bond between staff and students and among students across grade levels. The plan: a **7-period day once a month, with U-Knighted time during the 7th hour** — students arranged by grade level and divided among **41 teachers, about 17 students per group**. The committee meets before each session to write the lesson plan, focused on character development, diversity, motivation, community, goal setting "and FUN!!!" Assistant Principal Amy Buchanan, counselor Jen Hartenburg and social studies teacher Glen Rexer present.

The Board then recognizes **38 nominees** for the Outstanding Teacher Award, noting more nominations submitted by former and current students than ever before. Thirty-five receive certificates and plants; three were sent to Oakland Schools for the county-wide program: **Kimberly Phillips** (4th grade, Wattles) as Elementary Teacher of the Year, **Lindsey Becker** (7th grade math, Baker) as Middle School Teacher of the Year, and **Kristy Pierce** (social studies and economics, Athens, and Student Congress advisor) as High School Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the March 7 workshop, the March 21 meeting, and the March 23 special meeting, closed session and retreat, plus the February 2017 Treasurer's Report.

**What the March minutes record**
All seven members were present at the March 21 meeting and every resolution carried 7-0: Budget Amendment #2, Bid Pack 19 at $443,960.00, Bid Pack 20 at $1,044,052.90, the Brainard pool locker award, the General Painting award, and — as resolutions 17-033 and 17-034 — the district-owned property resolution that authorized investigating preservation of Section 1, marketing Section 11, developing the Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16, and appointing TMP Architecture.

On March 23 the Board met twice. A special meeting at 5:00 p.m. adopted resolution 17-035 going into closed session **to discuss district-owned properties** under Section 8(c) of the Open Meetings Act, on a unanimous roll call; the closed session ran from 5:05 to 6:16 p.m. with the superintendent and five administrators present and no other business conducted. The Board retreat followed at 6:26 p.m., covering a budget update on 2017-18 financial planning and cultural proficiency, adjourning at 9:05 p.m.

**Treasurer's Report — February 2017**
Total check disbursements are $6,087,180.55, the General Fund group $5,020,916.82 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,644,455.96. With $2,017,257.64 of wire transfers, $133,949.69 of P-Card purchases and $31,841.51 of ACH debits, less $7,991.67 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $8,262,237.72.

**Personnel**
A probationary contract for **Caitlin Bray**, 1.0 ASD program teacher at Boulan Park Middle School, holding a B.S. in special education from Central Michigan and an M.A. in applied behavior analysis and autism from Ball State expected July 2017, with prior experience at Metropolitan Nashville Public Schools and Huron Valley Schools.

**Business**

| Item | Award | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classroom A/V displays (RFP 9839) | VSC — $718,743.85 | 2016 Capital Projects |
| Synchronized clock system (RFP 9840) | Sound Engineering — $406,473.00 | 2016 Capital Projects |
| Container refuse collection | GFL Environmental USA, Inc. | 2017, 2018 and 2019 General Fund |
| Flooring replacement (RFP 9838) | Conventional Carpet, Inc. — $201,380.00 | Capital Maintenance |

**The A/V displays** drew three proposals opened March 10: Digital Age Technologies with Philips at $307,368.00 for middle schools only, VSC with SMART at $655,270.67 for high and middle schools, and Tierney Brothers with SMART and LG at $808,219.31. DAT is **not an authorized SMART reseller**, so it bid the middle schools alone. Convergent Technology Partners ran a technical demonstration with VSC on March 23 attended by the Technology Committee and all secondary principals.

The RFP had specified non-interactive flat panels in the middle schools and interactive panels in the high schools; the discussion that followed the demonstration turned on making them consistent across the secondary level, on individual departments' use of interactive displays to deepen learning, and on using an interactive display as a center or remediation station while other students work in groups — **"increasing the ability for a collaborative space not tied to the front of the room."** The recommended award therefore modifies VSC's base bid: **$655,270.67 base, plus $120,269.84 to upgrade the middle schools to interactive flat panels, less $56,796.66 of cabling — $718,743.85.** Completion is set for October 30.

**The clock system** drew four proposals: Sound Engineering with Sapling at $391,473.00, DAT with Carehawk at $403,787.00, I.COMM with Primex at $430,372.96 and Amcomm with Primex at $492,000.00. Sound Engineering, the low compliant bidder, confirmed the Sapling SBL31S4041R 4-digit digital clock; countdown functionality programmed **at no additional cost** for all secondary buildings at the principals' request; clocks showing hours and minutes normally, switching to minutes and seconds during countdown; hourly synchronization with the district time server; and integration with the existing PA system, correcting the PA clock daily at 2:00 A.M., also at no cost. Installation proceeds building by building, each cut over before the next begins, with completion by August 4.

Drawings for the transportation building were not available during the RFP, so no bidder priced it. The recommendation adds **an allowance of $15,000.00** to cover that building and any other clocks not discovered during the walk-through — $391,473.00 plus $15,000.00 for the $406,473.00 award.

**Flooring replacement** covers hallways, classrooms and music rooms at Athens, Troy High, IA East and Larson. Three bids were opened March 8; Conventional Carpet, Inc., which has done similar work for Troy and other Metro Detroit districts, was low qualified bidder, with a separate purchase order per site and completion by August 12, 2017.

**Other**
The Superintendent shares his **World Class by 2020** presentation from the previous week's workshop with the community.

Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: Smith Middle School's "U-Knighted Hour."** The previous summer, a group of interested teachers from Smith Middle School met to develop a homeroom for all Smith students. As a building, Smith had recognized the need to develop a stronger bond between staff and students, and among students between grade levels. The plan was to implement a 7-period day once a month and hold "U-Knighted" time during the 7th hour. Students were arranged by grade level and then divided among 41 teachers, resulting in approximately 17 students in each group. The committee meets before each U-Knighted Hour and develops a lesson plan for the groups, with the focus on character development, diversity, motivation, community, goal setting, "and FUN!!!" The program has been well received by students and staff alike. Amy Buchanan, Assistant Principal at Smith, counselor Jen Hartenburg and social studies teacher Glen Rexer are invited up to share more.

**Recognition 2.B: Oakland County Outstanding Teacher of the Year awards.** The Board recognizes the accomplishments of 38 individuals nominated for the Troy School District Outstanding Teacher Award Program. The nominees represent exemplary educators at the elementary, middle and high school levels, nominated by their peers and by parents, and this year the district received more nominations than ever submitted by former and current students. The nomination letters each described how the professionals honored go above and beyond to ensure their students learn, grow and thrive.

Thirty-five nominees receive certificates and plants: Adam Burns, TV production, English and Innovations at Athens; Amanda Hazergian, 2nd grade, Schroeder; Anne Drogosch, English language arts, Smith; Betsy Kennedy, English language arts, Baker; Brandon Preblich, physics, Athens; Cindy Christiansen, English language arts, Larson; Colette Carlin, 2nd grade, Hill; Dawn Hayes, special education resource room, Athens; Emily Beski, mathematics, IA East; Erica Conklin, special education, Barnard; Giovanna Marulli, 2nd grade, Hamilton; Gwen Simon, 4th grade, Barnard; Harriet Clark, communications, debate and English, Troy High; Jackie Losh, 1st grade, Schroeder; Jackie Skinner, 2nd grade, Wass; Janet Schoon, 5th grade instrumental music, Costello; Janice Boyer, 2nd grade, Hamilton; Jennifer Deward, 4th grade, Leonard; Julie Dagenais, 1st grade, Costello; Julie Marjamaa, kindergarten, Costello; Katherine Grabowski, special education, Larson; Kristen Marcaccio, kindergarten, Costello; Laurie Bussell, physical education, Bemis and Martell; Lindsey Gerbe, kindergarten, Barnard; Melinda Kaspari, 1st grade, Hill; Melissa Geeraerts, kindergarten, Hamilton; Melven Moffett, 2nd grade, Leonard; Nadeen Brown, 1st grade, Leonard; Nicole Given, kindergarten, Martell; and Trevor Potts, mathematics and technology, Larson, among others.

Three district nominees were sent to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the county-wide outstanding teacher award program administered by Oakland Schools: Kimberly Phillips, 4th grade teacher at Wattles Elementary, Elementary Teacher of the Year; Lindsey Becker, 7th grade math teacher at Baker Middle School, Middle School Teacher of the Year; and Kristy Pierce, social studies and economics teacher and Student Congress advisor at Athens High School, High School Teacher of the Year and Overall TSD Teacher of the Year. All three are invited to say a few words. Two of these names recur elsewhere in these packets: Dawn Hayes, among the nominees here, would appear with her family in the October 2018 "Protect the Vulnerable" Mission Moment, and Kristy Pierce would co-chair the district's Sex Education Advisory Board as an assistant principal at Boulan Park.

**Consent minutes: the March 7, 2017 workshop.** President Philippart called the workshop to order at 6:16 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — and administrators Superintendent Machesky, Deputy Superintendent Dziatczak, Griffor and others in attendance.

**Consent minutes: the March 21, 2017 regular meeting.** All seven members were present and every resolution carried 7-0. The minutes record the adoption of Budget Amendment #2; resolution 17-029 awarding Bid Pack 19 with $443,960.00 approved as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund; resolution 17-030 awarding bid pack 20 with $1,044,052.90 approved; resolution 17-031 awarding the pool locker replacement at Troy High to Brainard Enterprises; and resolution 17-032 awarding the interior painting to General Painting Company LLC.

Resolutions 17-033 and 17-034 carried the district-owned property item, the minutes reproducing its operative clauses: that the district authorizes administration to further investigate the preservation of the Section 1 property with the exception of the frontage, that the district authorizes the marketing of Section 11 property for purposes of sale, that the district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16, and that the district appoints TMP Architecture as architect of record and authorizes it to commence the design process. Board members were also guest judges at a Future Chef Competition; the meeting adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the March 23, 2017 special meeting and closed session.** President Philippart called the special meeting to order at 5:00 p.m. with all seven members present. Superintendent Machesky was in attendance along with Rick West, Rob Carson, Kris Griffor, Jordan Harris and Mark Dziatczak, and there were no members in the audience. There was no public communication. Resolution 17-035 provided that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Board shall go into closed session to discuss district-owned properties, on a roll call in which all seven members voted yes. The Board moved to closed session at 5:02 p.m. The special meeting minutes record the Board reconvening at 5:05 p.m. and adjourning at 5:03 p.m. — the two times are inconsistent as printed.

The closed session minutes record President Philippart calling it to order at 5:05 p.m. with all seven members present, Superintendent Machesky in attendance along with administrators Jordan Harris, Rick West, Kris Griffor, Mark Dziatczak, Rick West and Rob Carson (West listed twice as printed), and no other business conducted other than discussing district-owned properties. It adjourned at 6:16 p.m. — an hour and eleven minutes on the district's land, two days after the Board had adopted the resolution setting the disposition strategy in public.

**Consent minutes: the March 23, 2017 Board retreat.** President Philippart called it to order at 6:26 p.m. with all seven members present and administrators Machesky, Dziatczak, Harris, Griffor, Birmingham and West, plus approximately 6 other members of the audience. The agenda was public communication, a budget update on 2017-18 financial planning, and cultural proficiency. It adjourned at 9:05 p.m.

**Treasurer's Report, February 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $4,644,455.96, with Total General Fund of $5,020,916.82 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $6,087,180.55. Adding ACH debits of $31,841.51, outgoing wire transfers of $2,017,257.64 and P-Card purchases of $133,949.69, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $7,991.67, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $8,262,237.72. The middle sections of the packet are the February check register run by fund.

**Personnel 6.A: elementary and secondary.** The Board is recommended to approve a probationary contract for the 2016-2017 school year for Caitlin Bray, 1.0 ASD teacher at Boulan Park Middle School. Her biographical sketch records a B.S. in special education with a minor in integrated science from Central Michigan University, July 2013, and an M.A. in applied behavior analysis and autism from Ball State University expected July 2017; her teaching experience is with Metropolitan Nashville Public Schools in Antioch, Tennessee, as a special education teacher from July 2013 to May 2015, and with Huron Valley Schools in Highland, Michigan.

**Business 8.A: classroom A/V displays.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on classroom A/V displays, reviewed by Convergent Technology Partners. John C. Foster's April 11, 2017 evaluation and recommendation on RFP #9839 records that bids and proposals for classroom displays in the secondary school buildings were received, opened and publicly read at 1:30 P.M. on March 10, 2017, and that several mandatory alternates were requested for alternate solutions.

Three proposals were received: Digital Age Technologies with Philips displays at a base bid of $307,368.00, middle school only; VSC with SMART displays at $655,270.67 for high and middle schools; and Tierney Brothers with SMART and LG displays at $808,219.31 for high and middle schools. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution and acceptance of terms and conditions; all bidders provided compliant proposals and any exceptions or clarifications were deemed acceptable. The reason DAT's bid covers only part of the scope is stated plainly: DAT is not an authorized SMART reseller, therefore it only included the middle school displays in its response.

Further information and clarification were requested from bidders, and a technical demonstration and bid interview were conducted with VSC on March 23, 2017. The Technology Committee and all secondary principals attended the demonstration and remained afterward to discuss the potential solutions and options.

The clarifications and discussions recorded are substantive rather than procedural. The bid responses included non-interactive flat panel displays in the middle schools and interactive flat panel displays in the high schools, per the RFP requirements. Consideration of consistent interactive flat panel displays was discussed for the secondary level. Deep discussions were had regarding individual department use of interactive displays and the benefit to deepen learning. Discussions were also had regarding the ability to use the interactive display as a center or remediation station while other students are in work groups — therefore increasing the ability for a collaborative space not tied to the front of the room. The project includes an interactive flat panel display for all secondary classrooms that do not currently have a wall-mounted permanent display solution. VSC confirmed a single point of contact, a project manager, and daily online project updates to ensure project success, and confirmed it will meet the project schedule outlined in the RFP, completion October 30.

After final review, Convergent proceeded with the low compliant bidder, VSC, with the following modifications to the base bid response: base bid $655,270.67; upgrade middle schools to interactive flat panels, $120,269.84; deduct cabling, $56,796.66 — for a recommended award total of $718,743.85. The resolution awards the bid for classroom A/V displays to VSC in the amount of $718,743.85 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The pedagogical argument in the memo — that an interactive panel lets a teacher run a small group at a station while others work independently, rather than anchoring instruction to the front of the room — is what justifies spending an additional $120,269.84 to upgrade the middle schools beyond what the RFP itself required.

**Business 8.B: synchronized clock system.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on a complete, district-wide synchronized clock system, reviewed by Convergent Technology Partners. Foster's April 11, 2017 evaluation on RFP #9840 records that bids for a complete, turn-key, district-wide synchronized clock system were received, opened and publicly read at 2:30 P.M. on March 10, 2017, with no mandatory alternates requested.

Four proposals were received: Sound Engineering offering Sapling at a base bid of $391,473.00; Digital Age Technologies offering Carehawk at $403,787.00; I.COMM offering Primex at $430,372.96; and Amcomm offering Primex at $492,000.00. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution and acceptance of terms and conditions; all bidders provided compliant proposals and none took any exceptions. Further information and clarification were requested on March 16, 2017, and as all systems met the RFP requirements including the additional clarification, Convergent proceeded with the low compliant bidder, Sound Engineering.

The clarifications: the proposed digital clock is the Sapling model SBL31S4041R, a 4-digit model; countdown functionality is available and will be provided and programmed at no additional cost to the district for all secondary buildings as requested by the principals; digital clocks will show hours and minutes in normal mode, switch to minutes and seconds during countdown mode, then revert to normal mode after the countdown is complete; the clock system will synchronize with the district time server on an hourly basis; the clock system will integrate with the existing PA system and correct the PA system time once a day at 2:00 A.M., with PA system integration at no cost to the district; Sound Engineering confirmed a single point of contact, a project manager, and weekly online written status reports; and Sound Engineering confirmed it will meet the project schedule outlined in the RFP, completion August 4, with installation by building — once a building is complete it will be moved to the new system before implementation commences in the next building.

A note records a gap in the bid: drawings for the transportation building were not available during the RFP process and therefore pricing was not included in any proposal. Convergent requests an allowance of $15,000.00 to cover that building and any other clocks not discovered during the walk-through of district buildings. The recommendation is accordingly the base bid of $391,473.00 plus the $15,000.00 allowance, for a total of $406,473.00. The resolution awards the synchronized clock system to Sound Engineering in the amount of $406,473.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business 8.C: container refuse collection services.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on district-wide container refuse collection services, reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations. The resolution awards the bid to GFL Environmental USA, Inc. based on their bid response, approved as an expenditure of the 2017, 2018 and 2019 General Fund — the only award in the packet stated without a dollar figure in the resolution, and the only one spanning three fiscal years.

**Business 8.D: floor replacement.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on flooring replacement work at Athens and Troy High Schools, International Academy East and Larson Middle School, reviewed by Rob Carson. His March 29, 2017 memorandum on RFP 9838 records that the scope is to provide flooring removal, floor preparation, and materials and installation of new flooring to hallways, classrooms and music rooms as detailed in the bid specifications for each school; that on March 8 three bids were opened, which resulted in Conventional Carpet, Inc. being identified as the low qualified bidder; and that Conventional Carpet has performed similar work for the Troy School District and for other school districts in the Metro Detroit area. He requests a total project cost award of $201,380.00, with a separate purchase order created for each site project, and a completion date of August 12, 2017. The resolution awards the flooring replacement to Conventional Carpet, Inc. in the amount of $201,380.00 as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.

**Other 10.A: World Class by 2020.** Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. writes to the Board on April 18, 2017 that the Superintendent will share his presentation on "World Class by 2020" from the previous week's workshop with the community at that evening's Board meeting. The report is the public version of the strategic framing that recurs throughout these packets — the district's journey to become a World Class School District by 2020, and the four characteristics of world class that would later be cited in the Early Childhood Center naming resolution.

Read as a whole, the April 2017 packet is the district equipping its buildings. The two technology awards together come to more than a million dollars from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, and both were shaped in the evaluation rather than in the bid: the display project grew by $120,269.84 because the principals and Technology Committee decided, after seeing a demonstration, that middle schools should get the same interactive panels as the high schools, and the clock project grew by $15,000.00 because nobody had drawings for the transportation building. Around those, the meeting hires one autism-program teacher, replaces flooring in four buildings, contracts three years of refuse collection, and honors 38 teachers and a middle school that decided its students needed a homeroom.
